title: MB4-05395
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Kosovo, is appealing against a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Kosovo, is appealing against a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
He did not present new evidence in support of his appeal, nor is he requesting that a hearing be held before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).

Pursuant to subsection 111(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD, namely, that XXXX XXXX is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.

The appellant is a 24-year-old man who alleges in his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), which he submitted to the RPD, that he started his own business on XXXX XXXX, 2012, opening up a XXXX shop in the municipality of XXXX.

The appellant alleges that on June 1, 2012, unknown armed men entered his XXXX shop and threatened him, demanding 700 euros per month to avoid [translation] "problems." He alleges that he had informed the police, who apparently replied that it was normal for a shopkeeper to pay [translation] "extortion money."

The appellant alleges that he paid the first 700 euros on June 15, 2012, and continued to do so every month thereafter. He alleges that, on August 30, 2013, the criminals demanded that he start paying 1,000 euros every month.

The appellant alleges that he decided to close his XXXX shop, which he did on XXXX XXXX, 2013. He alleges that he went to live for a month in the city of XXXX with his uncles, before returning home until he left his country on XXXX XXXX, 2013. He passed through Germany and the Dominican Republic before he arrived in Canada, using a false passport, on April 19, 2014, and claimed refugee protection here.

In light of the copy of the business register and photographs entered into evidence, the RPD believed that the XXXX shop mentioned by the appellant existed and that he worked there, but still found that the appellant did not testify in a straightforward manner and that contradictions and inconsistencies in the evidence undermined the credibility of his allegation that he had been threatened and extorted from for the following reasons: - he testified that his brother was the one registered as the owner of the XXXX shop, contrary to what his previous allegations suggested; - his brother, the owner of the XXXX shop, had never been threatened, not even after the XXXX shop closed; and - he failed to state in his BOC Form that individuals were looking for him in Kosovo after he left the country.

Before the RAD, the appellant submits that the RPD erred in that his testimony was in fact clear; his statement that he was the owner of the XXXX shop when his brother was is not [translation] "nonsense" since he was the one taking care of the shop; it is wrong to find that the extortionists have no interest in him given that his brother, the owner of the XXXX shop, has not been bothered by them; and he testified that he was not sure whether the individuals who were looking for him after he left the country were the extortionists.

For these reasons, the appellant requests that the RAD set aside the RPD's determination and [translation] "render a favourable decision" or, alternatively, refer the matter to the RPD for re-determination.
The IRPA does not expressly set out the standard of review or intervention to be applied by the RAD when reviewing decisions rendered by the RPD.

In this case, the appellant submits in his memorandum that the appeal before the RAD should be similar to a de novo appeal rather than to the standards of review used by the Federal Court in judicial review, although he states in paragraph 102 of the memorandum that the RPD's credibility findings are [translation] "clearly unreasonable." I agree with the appellant in part.

The Federal Court, which has the authority to review the RAD's decisions, has rendered several decisions to date concerning the RAD's standard of review or intervention or its role when an RPD decision is appealed to it.
In Alvarez1 and Eng,2 both rendered on July 17, 2014, the Honourable Justice Shore of the Federal Court of Canada has ruled on this matter.

In paragraphs 28 and 29 in Alvarez, and paragraphs 29 and 30 of Eng, the Court writes the following: [28] Parliament conferred a true appellate function on the RAD, a specialized (if not overspecialized) tribunal, which sits on appeal of the decisions of another administrative tribunal. Contrary to a court exercising a superintending and reforming power over public bodies, the RAD's primary responsibility is to ensure the integrity and consistency of proceedings before the RPD and to reduce needless duplication of proceedings (including before the Federal Court). When analyzing a decision of the RPD, the RAD must not merely determine whether it was made in a reasonable manner, but, rather, analyze whether the RPD relied on a wrong principle of law or misassessed the facts to the point of making a palpable and overriding error (Housen, above). [29] "Palpable and overriding error" is often used interchangeably with the "clearly wrong" or "unreasonable" decision test. However, this is the appellate-level standard of intervention that a specialized appeal tribunal such as the RAD must apply when reviewing a decision and not the judicial review standard of reasonableness. Even though there are similarities, these standards are different.

In paragraph 33 of Alvarez and paragraph 34 of Eng, the Court adds the following: [33] The Court agrees that the RPD, as the tribunal of first instance, is owed a measure of deference with regard to its findings of fact, and of fact and law. The RPD is better situated to draw such conclusions as it is the tribunal of first instance, the trier of facts, having the advantage of hearing testimony viva voce (Housen, above). However, the RAD must nonetheless perform its own assessment of all of the evidence in order to determine whether the RPD relied on a wrong principle of law or misassessed the facts to the point of making a palpable and overriding error. The idea that the RAD may substitute an original decision by a determination that should have been rendered without first assessing the evidence is completely inconsistent with the purpose of the IRPA and the case law dealing with the virtually identical wording of subsection 67(2). The Court finds that the RAD misinterpreted its role as an appeal body in holding that its role was merely to assess, against a standard of reasonableness, whether the RPD's decision is within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes.

In Huruglica,3 rendered on August 22, 2014, the Honourable Justice Phelan of the Federal Court examines the role and functions of the RAD and writes: [44] Subject to specific language, the need for deference, for example, is less compelling between the RAD and the RPD than it is between the judiciary and the executive. The relationship is more akin to that between a trial court and an appellate court but further influenced by the much greater remedial powers given to the appellate tribunal. [45] Therefore, a standard of review analysis is not an appropriate analytical approach....

In considering the RAD's authority under subsection 111(1) of the IRPA to substitute a determination that, "in its opinion, should have been made," Justice Phelan writes: [47] Unlike judicial review, the RAD, pursuant to subsection 111(1)(b), may substitute the determination which "in its opinion, should have been made". One precondition of exercising this power is that the RAD must conduct an independent assessment of the application in order to arrive at its own opinion. It is not necessary, in order to trigger this remedial power, that the RAD must find error on some standard of review basis. [48] The restriction on the ability to receive fresh evidence is not a bar to conducting a de novo appeal....

Justice Phelan finally concludes that: [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision. [55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is a "palpable and overriding error".
In Spasoja,4 rendered on September 23, 2014, the Honourable Justice Roy of the Federal Court also examines the RAD's role.

In that decision, the Court first found, in line with the previous decisions in Huruglica, Eng and Alvarez, that the RAD erred in applying the reasonableness standard of review rather than conducting an independent assessment of the claim for refugee protection (paragraph 12).

The Honourable Justice Roy proceeds with a detailed analysis of the statutory provisions concerning the RAD under the IRPA; of the case law pertaining to the role of an appellate body within an administrative tribunal, specifically Parizeau;5 and of Parliament's intent as stated by various stakeholders in debates about the RAD before the parliamentary committee of the House of Commons to determine that the appeal referred to in sections 110 and 111 of the IRPA cannot be equated to a judicial review but, rather, to an appeal in its own right (paragraph 39).

Relying on the conclusions in Parizeau with respect to the standard of review to be applied by an appeal tribunal, the Honourable Justice Roy, distinguishing himself from his colleague who rendered the Court's decision in Huruglica, concludes that the standards of review to be applied by the RAD are correctness for questions of law, and palpable and overriding error for questions of fact and questions of mixed law and fact. Moreover, the RAD must show deference to the RPD's findings regarding the credibility given to the witnesses heard by it (paragraphs 39, 40 and 46).

The Honourable Justice Roy also states that he could not find any indicators providing for an appeal de novo before the RAD (paragraph 42) and writes in the following paragraph of his decision that: [43] Instead, the scheme under review addresses appeals on specific questions, be it of fact, of law or of mixed law and fact (subsection 110(1)). In my view, that means that the appellant must identify the questions on which the appeal will focus. It will be on the basis of the record of proceedings before the RPD that the appeal will be heard based on the questions identified and raised, subject to the documentary evidence (subsection 110(3)) or evidence that is consistent with subsection 110(4)....

Lastly, in a decision rendered on October 8, 2014 (Alyafi v. M.C.I., 2014 FC 952), the Honourable Justice Martineau of the Federal Court, after reviewing the above decisions, first concludes that they all reject the reasonableness standard of review and subsequently states that, in his opinion, the RAD must be allowed to choose between the two remaining approaches, namely, the one outlined in Eng, Alvarez and Spasoja, which is the standard of palpable and overriding error, and the one outlined in Huruglica, which he describes as "a composite and variable standard of review resulting from the nature of the claim before the RAD-characterized as a hybrid appeal-and the particular nature of questions of fact, or of mixed fact and law, raised by an appellant" (paragraph 16).

At paragraph 46 of Alyafi, Justice Martineau writes the following: [46] ... I chose the middle path, that of wisdom: allow the RAD to apply the second or third approach as long as the question of the scope of the appellate review of the RPD's decisions has not been settled by a final judgment by the Federal Court of Appeal or the Supreme Court of Canada. Quite simply.

Accordingly, I am of the opinion that it is preferable for the RAD to apply the principles set out in Spasoja in this case given that no new evidence was submitted and no hearing was held before the RAD. However, I am also of the opinion that, in this case, I would come to the same conclusion by applying the principles set out in Huruglica.

I am of the opinion that the error alleged by the appellant in the RPD's assessment of his credibility is a question of fact and, therefore, subject to the standard of palpable and overriding error. I would grant a measure of deference to the RPD's findings with respect to the credibility of the witness, the appellant, whom it had the privilege of hearing and seeing before it.
However, I will be conducting a review and my own assessment of all the evidence presented before the RPD to determine whether the RPD committed any errors.

At paragraph 91 of Parizeau, a palpable and overriding error is described as follows: [translation] [91] ... A palpable and overriding error is an error that, in its undeniability-and therefore not a difference of opinion on the assessment of the evidence-determines the outcome of the dispute in that the conclusion of the trier of fact, that is, the result of his or her decision, cannot hold water, thus, ipso facto, making the decision unreasonable.
The issue in this case is whether the RPD erred in its assessment of the appellant's credibility.

Having assessed all the evidence submitted to the RPD, including the recording of the hearing that was held before it, and in light of the RPD's reasons and the appellant's memorandum, I am of the opinion that the answer to that question is no, for the following reasons.
Just like the RPD, I am also of the opinion that the evidence submitted contains contradictions and implausibilities that are major enough to undermine the appellant's credibility.

The first one has to do with the appellant's business, which allegedly is the source of his fear of returning to his country. After the review of Exhibit P-3, which is a certificate of registration that does not indicate who the owner of the business is, the appellant was asked whether any documents demonstrating that he was the owner of the business existed. The appellant responded that those documents demonstrate that the owner was his older brother. He indicated that it was the [translation] "tradition" in his country for the older brother to be the owner of the younger brother's business. When asked to explain why he wrote in his BOC Form that [translation] "I started my own business," the appellant responded that he was the one working there and running it.

In my view, this contradiction or failure to mention that his brother was the owner of the business undermines the appellant's credibility. The matter of business ownership is all the more important because, as I will mention later, it is likely that the owner of the business would be targeted by the extortionists, and that he is the one who will likely be pursued, if anyone is, after the closure of the business.

Furthermore, the appellant's failure to mention in his BOC Form, or to add at the beginning of the hearing when he had the opportunity to do so, that the strangers came looking for him at his home in Kosovo, after he left the country, in January 2014, is also an omission that, in my opinion, undermines his credibility. The fact that criminals are looking for him is the very basis of his fear of returning to Kosovo. In his memorandum, the appellant states that this omission was because he was not sure whether those individuals who went to his home were the extortionists. I cannot accept that argument since, to the contrary, the appellant testified that he believes that those were the extortionists based on the description provided by his father, who met them, and further explained when questioned about it that he [translation] "does not know why" he did not write it down on his form.

Finally, I am also of the opinion that the fact that the appellant's brother, who is the registered owner of the XXXX shop, was never bothered by anyone in Kosovo also undermines the credibility of the appellant's fear. On that matter, the RPD concluded, in paragraph 18 of its reasons, that this demonstrates that the appellant, even if he had been the subject of extortion in the past, is no longer of interest to the extortionists.

In my view, that is the most important point in the RPD's decision, on which I agree. Even if it is credible that the appellant worked in a XXXX shop and was forced to pay a monthly amount to extortionists, I am of the opinion that the evidence presented shows that there is no serious possibility or probability that the extortionists would have any interest in going after the appellant if he were to return to his country.

That conclusion is based on a number of factors. First, no one even tried to go after the owner of the XXXX shop, the appellant's brother, whose name appears on the documents for the XXXX shop and who is easily found in the village where he lives and where the appellant lived. Furthermore, nothing demonstrates that the appellant himself was being sought. As mentioned above, the appellant's credibility regarding the individuals who allegedly appeared at his house looking for him is undermined by the omission of that fact in the BOC Form. In addition, the appellant states in his memorandum that he is not sure that those individuals were the extortionists.

I add that, although the appellant is not required to explain someone else's actions, it still seems implausible to me that the extortionists are still interested in the appellant now that the XXXX shop is closed, since, as he testified, all the shopkeepers must pay a monthly amount to extortionists. Since he is no longer a shopkeeper, it seems unlikely that the extortionists have any interest whatsoever in going after him. All they will have to do is extort the next shopkeeper who will take over the location the appellant was occupying.

Similarly, it is implausible that the extortionists waited until January 2014, four months after the XXXX shop closed, to go to the appellant's home and find out about him. Finally, I note that, on the date of the hearing, in September 2014, the appellant had no other indication from family members or anyone else that individuals were looking for him in Kosovo. He also did not submit additional evidence before the RAD on that matter.
In light of all the above, I conclude that the appellant did not demonstrate that the RPD made a palpable and overriding error in its decision that would warrant the intervention of the RAD.

For these reasons, I confirm the determination of the RPD, namely that XXXX XXXX is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.

The appeal is dismissed. Normand Leduc Normand Leduc July 6, 2015 Date IRB translation Original language: French 1 Alvarez v. M.C.I., 2014 F.C. 702. 2 Eng v. M.C.I., 2014 F.C. 711. 3 Huruglica v.
